items.title: Sakura Tsuruta
items.author: Flow State
items.content: It’s Friday so we’re listening to something more upbeat. Today we’re listening to Sakura Tsuruta, a Japanese electronic musician from Tokyo. She studied classical piano growing up, and became interested in the therapeutic application of music in high school when her grandfather faced dementia. At Berklee College of Music she studied music therapy and electronic production; she thereafter worked at a hospice, using music in palliative care. That experience led her to start making music herself, in which she fuses her classical background and electronic production techniques. We’re starting with her 2024 LP, , a collection of eight tracks that combine driving bass lines, precise percussion, and melodic arpeggios and leads. We’re also playing her 2022 LP,

items.title: Jeremiah Chiu (Interview)
items.author: Flow State
items.content:
Today we’re listening to Jeremiah Chiu, a Taiwanese-American synthesist and composer from Chicago. He took up piano and violin at age five, and went on to play keys in bands (pop punk), leading to an interest in synths. Now based in Los Angeles, Chiu creates fascinating synth compositions, often on interesting instruments. His 2023 album, , was made at the Vintage Synthesizer Museum in Los Angeles. He’s a member of the electro-jazz quintet SML, contributing modular synths to the group’s virtuosic live improvisations (see example on YouTube), or their “five-person dialogues” as he called them. On his new album, , he mixes arpeggiated synth with drum machines, acoustic drums (by Booker Stardrum and Ben Lumsdaine), viola (Marta Sofia Honer), saxophone (Patrick Shiroishi), and more. “A large part of the studio process is experimenting by taking improvisations or other performances and using them as material for new pieces,” he told us. “I also use these samples to re-synthesize things – i.e. as a carrier voice for a vocoder or as an envelope follower or any other idiosyncratic way of taking one thing and using it to transform something else.” A conversation with Jeremiah follows the streaming links.

What’s your earliest memory of music?

It was very cute. I remember my parents and I would call my grandparents on holidays or to occasionally catch up – I must have been 3 or 4 – and at the end of each call I would sing Stevie Wonder’s “I Just Called to Say I Love You” to them. Because of that, the song has a permanent spot in my memory and life. As a teenager, I remember learning this song to cover in my pop punk band. Maybe it’s time I do a version.

What was your first instrument and how did you get started with synths?

I started playing piano and violin at age five or so. I took private lessons on both instruments and eventually joined the junior high orchestra as well as a regional youth orchestra in the Chicagoland area. In high school, I decided not to continue playing in orchestra. It’s something I regret now, but at the time, I started learning guitar and bass and wanted to hang out with my peers in punk bands – a pretty normal desire for a highschooler in the suburbs, I assume.

Near the end of high school, all of the friends I had were in bands and equally into punk, emo, and rave culture. Chicago House and Detroit Techno were hugely inspirational and analog (vintage) synthesizers were cheap and plentiful. We were playing in emo punk bands – starting to incorporate synths – and also learning how to beatmatch drum machines to tracks on a turntable. At the time, you could buy a synth (something like a Roland Juno-106) for $100. It provided us with the opportunity to try out a bunch of different synthesizers and sell and trade them easily. A friend, Mike Bingaman, lent me his MC-505 Groovebox and that really got me interested in sequencing, programming synths, and connecting the instruments to each other through MIDI and CV/Gate.

In retrospect, it was a unique experience to have so many teenagers in a community that was really open to a lot of music and art.

What were your first recordings like? What did you use to make them?

My sister had this Casio WK-1200 that wasn’t being used. It sat in our dining room, next to the kitchen. When my parents would be fixing dinner, I would sit on that thing and make songs. It had the ability to record up to six parts using internal sounds. So I learned to make a drum part, bass part, chords, and lead parts. It really taught me how to put parts of a song together. I also spent a lot of time making mixtapes by recording snippets of radio onto boombox that had a record function. I still work like this quite a bit, except I use live performance as my “radio.”

Once I was in bands, we – like so many people – had a Tascam 4-track recorder and a single microphone. We learned how to record parts and bus them down to single tracks to add more tracks. From there, the evolution went a bit like this: a 16-track minidisc recorder, a Fostex digital recorder, a Compaq computer with Cubase controlled by a 12-track MIDI console, a Pro Tools MBox with that goofy dongle. All of the early recording experiments were done on cassette tape or CD.

What early artists/albums were most influential to you finding your own sound?

Isotope 217, Tortoise, and the whole “post rock” Chicago scene were and still are huge influences. I’m grateful and honestly in disbelief that I call a lot of those people friends and collaborators now. Beyond the sound of the albums and music, the proliferation of different groups within a community reminded me of other thriving music scenes, like ‘70s Dusseldorf, Cologne, and Berlin scenes and ‘80s downtown New York scenes.

I love looking at liner notes and personnel on albums and seeing a rotating cast of similar characters – especially when those relationships traverse mediums. In particular, I remember being in art school and finding out that Steve Reich and Sol Lewitt were close friends. Moments like that blew my mind because I grew up in a culture where everything seemed to have a defined boundary. Music was Genre, Art was Movements. But the actuality was much more fluid, hybrid, and boundaryless.

Ultimately, the goal is to participate in, and support a thriving artistic community where artists can come together, be in dialogue with each other and contribute positively to our understanding and experience of the world.

What was your studio setup for ? What instruments/gear/software did you use to make it?

I work in Ableton. All of the contributors on the album recorded remotely and then I edited and arranged the material. More than once, a drum take would get resampled or sliced and it would form an entirely new track. For me, a large part of the studio process is experimenting by taking improvisations or other performances and using them as material for new pieces. I also use these samples to re-synthesize things – i.e. as a carrier voice for a vocoder or as an envelope follower or any other idiosyncratic way of taking one thing and using it to transform something else.

In my modular rig, I have several samplers and oscillators that I use to create percussion and melody. The samplers are all routed via my mixer’s aux send, so at any given moment, I can sample something and work with that.

Only recently have I started to incorporate software synths as a way to work out some of the compositions in MIDI before recording them again with analog synthesizers. On this record, I used my modular synth rig, Roland gear (101, 202, 303, 606, 808), Moog Matriarch, and a few sample-based organs or pads that I made. Beyond that, Marta Sofia Honer (viola), Marquis Hill (trumpet), Patrick Shiroishi (saxophone), Ben Lumsdaine (drums), Booker Stardrum (drums), Takako Minekawa (voice & field recordings), and Will Miller (EVI) all contributed to the album.

How did your experience with SML affect your solo work?

SML has been a great experience in listening and making intentional moves. Josh (in SML) has talked about it as being a mode of self-producing, or live producing. I think what he means is that when we’re playing live, it’s all improvised, but since it’s a performance, we’re balancing risk-taking with intentionality. Every sound each of us brings to the table is a part of a five-person dialogue. However, each of us has the opportunity to shift the conversation as it’s moving, because we all respond.

In my solo work, I improvise a lot in performances. This is usually done with live-sampling and sequencing. With sequencers in my modular rig, I often have a sequence sequencing a sequence. To clarify, instead of sending a sequencer a steady clock pulse, I’m sending it a rhythmic sequence. This starts to articulate and move the sequence I’ve written in ways that are unexpected and forces me to listen, adjust, and react. What I’m interested in is having some volatility in the performance. An opportunity to have things go awry that force me to be present.

With my previous solo album, , it felt very close to how SML currently operates. It was collection of improvisations that was then edited down into an album. With I intentionally swung the pendulum in the other direction. Instead of build the record based on improvisations, I wanted to compose some pieces from the ground up. Some of the songs were still born out of an improvisation, but I challenged myself to explore the album in a way that I hadn’t been doing with my other groups (SML, Marta Sofia Honer duo, and Jeff Parker Expansion Trio).

You’re also a graphic designer and educator. What are some examples, if any, of your work in those disciplines affecting your music, or vice versa?

When people ask if there’s overlap between my art, design, and music practice, I always talk about the vocabulary as a way to understand how similar they are. In all of the creative fields, we can talk about composition, narrative, contrast, tensions, rhythmic, dynamics, etc… While we generally pin art and design towards a more visual realm, and music to be more sonic, I don’t really separate them that way. When I make an album, I always approach it like a film, or narrative work. I’m thinking about the pacing from the beginning to the end. I’m thinking about the tension and release and the changes between songs as opportunities to carry a listener through a series of ideas tethered to one larger concept.

In a more direct example, some years ago I was commissioned by The Getty Center in LA to create a score for a player piano as part of their performance, Pianographs. The player piano score rolls vertically across the face of the piano as the music is played. Holes punched in the paper scroll activate notes. Because the scroll was such a visual part of the performance, my approach to the composition was to compose the score by drawing images and words onto the scroll. I was less worried about the exact harmony, melody, or counterpoint, and more interested in hearing how these images and text came to life through sound.

Name an underrated artist from the past 50 years.

I’m not sure if Franco Battiato classifies as underrated as he became one of Italy’s most famous singers. However, his early experimental records , , , etc. are all so incredible, and I’m always surprised that they’re not more widely recognized by today’s selectors. Go listen to them!

What are you working on next?

I feel so grateful to have the support of International Anthem and to be collaborating with so many incredible artists in our wonderful community. In the coming year, I’m continuing the work with SML, Marta, and Jeff Parker in hopes that one or more of those will finish another album. At this very moment, I’m about to send this interview off and record on an amazing track for Marquis Hill.

items.title: Across the Horizon Ep. 73: Mary Lattimore
items.author: Flow State
items.content:
On today’s episode of Across the Horizon, Bob Holmes of the band SUSS is joined by harpist and composer Mary Lattimore, one of the curators of Across the Horizon Volume 2. They talk about her contributions to the series as well as those of her guests, Nailah Hunter and Meg Baird. Mary also brought along a playlist of music she’s been listening to the Italian village of Tatti, her new part-time home. The playlist includes Yo La Tengo, Windsor for the Derby, Daniel Ogren, and more.

Collected Pieces: 2015-2020 is a great survey of her work, showcasing the way she manipulates the harp sound with pedals to create atmospheres of profundity. , her collaboration with vocalist and composer Julianna Barwick, came out in January. They recorded in a Paris museum, Lattimore using three golden harps from the 18th and 19th century and Barwick using synths and a vocoder. “It was terrifying to hear the cracks when tuning the harps; they’re very delicate instruments,” she tells Bob on the show. “You think about the person who played them last, the person who initially built them…”

items.title: Flow State Episode 349
items.author: Flow State
items.content:
Today’s mix includes three Ryuichi Sakamoto tracks from across three different decades, inspired by his memoir . We play a moving track from the Adam Wiltzie and Jóhann Jóhannsson record and a longform ambient piece by Blanket Swimming. There are a few harp recordings which function as a preview of tomorrow’s guest on Across the Horizon. We picked a single from Andrew W.K.’s jazzy, strange new record (h/t ). The BPM accelerates with Stella Z, Damian Dalla Torre, and Loidis. The final track is a new ambient work by Toro y Moi. We hope you enjoy.

items.title: Adam Wiltzie (Interview)
items.author: Flow State
items.content:
Today we’re listening to Adam Wiltzie, an American ambient musician from New York City. We recommended his solo music in 2024 and his project Stars of the Lid (with the late Brian McBride) twicebefore. Wiltzie himself has done a number of notable collaborations including The Dead Texan with Christina Vantzou and A Winged Victory for the Sullen with Dustin O’Halloran. In 2013, Wiltzie entered the studio with Jóhann Jóhannsson, and over a few years the two would create several “orchestral psychedelic drone compositions.” In 2018, Jóhannsson passed away, and after some years passed, Wiltzie returned to the project with the blessing of Jóhannsson’s family. He re-recorded guitar parts with Steve Albini in Chicago, electronics with Tim Hecker, and orchestral strings in Budapest. Friendship Survival Guide is the resulting record, which came out in September. “The one thing I still feel listening to this,” Wiltzie told us, “is that JJ still sounds so alive to me.” We’re also revisiting by Stars of the Lid. A conversation with Adam follows the streaming links.

What’s your earliest memory of music?

It would have been the spring of 1972. I was playing around the apartment in the upper east side of Manhattan & fell in my parents bedroom hitting the corner of their bed severely cutting my bottom lip, as my mother took me down & jumped in a taxi to the emergency room I remember the driver blasting “Rocket Man” by Elton John, I will never forget it…

What were your first recordings like? What did you use to make them?

My four-track tape machine at the dawn of the 1990s cost $300, and that was a fortune for me considering I lived in squalor. The sounds we created on these recorders were essential to the sounds we were creating at the time & was the catalyst for Stars of the Lid’s early textural aura.

How did you first get into ambient music?

My first love & major influence was Brian Eno, hard to say there was anyone else that taught me conceptually about how to get in the middle of your ideas, let go of your option paralysis move forward, than the great bald one.

You’ve collaborated with several composers best known for their film scores – Jóhannsson but also Dustin O’Halloran. Stars of the Lid music has been used in film and TV as well. Was Stars of the Lid and your other work influenced by scores?

No, not at all. I am guessing by your question you have never listened to Stars of the Lid? I would also propose that Friendship Survival Guide was not either, it just happened to be the catalyst that started our collaboration. Most of the time when you are scoring films it can be really uninspiring & what was originally going to be this specific sounding entity usually turns into this strange sculpture that is cobbled together by different producers pushing through arbitrary ideas that they feel are an important part of the storytelling process.

What are some similarities and differences in composing for film versus making standalone records?

The biggest difference is composing for film will always fall in the category of “commissioned work,” so essentially it will never be just for yourself. There is always another sentient being that will have a say in the final outcome. This is not always a negative, but the sooner you let go & realise this, you will spend less time fretting about the occasional rejection of your work & ideas.

One of the moving things about Friendship Survival Guide is that listening to it now, knowing the context, it evokes loss, grief, memory, and nostalgia. Yet most of the original material was recorded with Jóhannsson himself. What was your experience revisiting the original recording with not only his memory but also Steve Albini’s in mind?

There was a bit of anxiety leading up to the moment I dived back in but once I started creating again from the palette of sounds we made all those years ago I would say the experience was mostly pleasant, inspiring & rather cathartic. Not sad at all, as the one thing I still feel listening to this is that JJ still sounds so alive to me.

What were the first and second studio setups for this record? What instruments/gear/software did you use during the original collaboration and later completion of the record?

I suppose there were 4 major events to the recording.

#1 was the initial ideas that were recorded between 2013-2017. A lot of these were tape loops that were recorded on a Studer 2 inch 16 track machine, so that we could have our initial loops with multitracks of layers. Then next step was bouncing the loops down to another Studer machine but this one was 2 track 1/2 inch. This also gave us the ability to crush the multitracks a bit. A final bounce was then activated to Johann’s Revox 1/4inch machine & these ended with another layer of tape compression as it starts to get really nasty sounding by the time you shrink the bandwidth from 2 inch to 1/4 inch. Then we digitised & this is what you hear on the recording

#2 was a few years ago when I started to put the pieces together & started to create the arcs that would finish the pieces. This next major event was recording the guitars & re-amping of the tape loops in Chicago with Steve Albini @ Electrical Audio. We used Sovtek MIG 50’s heads through Marshall cabinets with Coles STC 4038 Ribbon mics for the close & Josephson C 617 condensers for the rooms & Steve laid them on the floor, which is a technique I never attempted but they sound incredible for my ears.

#3 was orchestrating the strings & recording in Budapest. We used 24 players & recorded everything in 4 hours.

#4 is the final & most essential which was the final mix with my long time collaborator Francesco Donadello (won a Grammy for his work on the series soundtrack)

How do you discover new music these days? Any recent notable finds?

I am basically forever an inveterate used record collector. I don’t engage in actively seeking out new music from this era, but I am continually fascinated by how much music still exists from the past I have never listened to.

A couple recent finds from the past few years as I am in the middle of some kind of jazz resurgence in my head are Donald Byrd / Electric Byrd & Freddie Hubbard / Red Clay.

Name an underrated artist from the past 50 years.

I am not exactly sure what underrated means as it is forever being used in sports analogy, but for music in my collection it would have to be Robert Hampson.

What are you working on next?

For the moment it is the new A Winged Victory for the Sullen, hopefully it will be released before the end of 2027.

items.title: Djrum
items.author: Flow State
items.content: It’s Friday so we’re listening to something more upbeat. Today we’re listening to Djrum, an English electronic musician and DJ. It’s pronounced “drum.” We recommended Djrum’s album last year, which ended up landing on our best of 2025 list. Djrum is a talented producer but he’s an even more talented DJ. His all-vinyl sets are marathons of eclecticism, of which there are several examples on YouTube, the standout being the Tower Bridge show he did with Fabric in 2021. Last week he released a record, which he recorded on vinyl and then lightly edited and overdubbed. The 82-minute journey is all over the place, “from orchestral breakcore to field recordings, and from spaced-out jungle to the nastiest bass rumblings,” as wrote in Pitchfork. We’re also giving another listen afterward.

items.title: Hermanos Gutiérrez
items.author: Flow State
items.content: Today we’re listening to Hermanos Gutiérrez, Ecuadorian-Swiss guitarists Alejandro and Estevan. We recommended them in 2024 and 2023. Estevan started playing guitar in elementary school, focusing on milonga (Argentinian folk) and classical; later on, Alejandro taught himself guitar. The brothers started playing together regularly after a spontaneous jam session at Alejandro’s apartment. Hermanos Gutiérrez formed on a trip to the American southwest, specifically the Mojave Desert and Death Valley; “the desert is where our music was born,” Estevan told Premier Guitar. Their new record, , came out in September. The idea for the record occurred to the brothers upon seeing a 1973 photo of their dad in Machu Picchu; throughout, Estevan plays the nylon guitar his father gave him at eight years old. The cinematic and evocative tracks are odes to the Andean mountain landscape. We’re also revisiting their 2024 record, , which has more of a psychedelic sound, as the title suggests. Both records were produced by Dan Auerbach of the Black Keys.
